prompt: Match each function to the decision it makes.
hint: Four functions, four kinds of decision.

pairs.right: Where money goes and when bills are paid
Which customers to reach, and how
How much stock to hold and how to deliver
Whom to hire and how to keep them

prompt: Of every R$ 100 Varanda's customers paid in 2025, how much was left as operating profit?

choices.why: That is what is left after paying for the goods, before running the company: the gross margin.
Right: an operating margin of 2.9%, which is why small changes in large flows decide the year.
That is the share of sales spent on people.
That is the cost of goods as a share of sales.

prompt: Stock rose 12%. Why does the lesson say an analyst should know who is reading before reporting it?
hint: A risk, a relief, a promise.

choices.text: Only finance is allowed to see stock figures
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson restricts stock figures; they mean different things to different readers.

choices.text: A risk to finance, a relief to operations, a promise to marketing
choices.why: Right: the same number answers a different question for each function.

choices.text: A 12% rise is too small to matter to anybody
choices.why: At R$ 9.48 million of stock, 12% is over a million reais tied up.

choices.text: Stock belongs in days of cover, never in a percentage
choices.why: Days are useful, but the lesson's point here is the reader, not the unit.

prompt: In your income statement, what is Varanda's gross margin for 2025, in percent to one decimal?
What are Varanda's 2025 operating expenses, in thousands of reais?
hint: The sum of the five lines between gross profit and operating profit.

prompt: Put the lines of the simplified income statement in order, from top to bottom.
hint: Sales at the top, profit at the bottom.
trap: Putting operating expenses before gross profit mixes the cost of the goods with the cost of running the company.

prompt: A R$ 6,000 sofa is sold in December on ten interest-free instalments. How does it appear in December?
hint: Profit is recorded when the sale happens.

choices.text: R$ 600 of sales in December, and R$ 600 in each of the next nine months
choices.why: That describes the cash, not the sale.

choices.text: All R$ 6,000 in December's sales; the cash over ten months
choices.why: Right: the income statement records the sale when it happens; the bank account fills slowly.

choices.text: Nothing until the last instalment is paid
choices.why: The sale and its margin are December's, whatever the payment terms.

choices.text: As a cost, since Varanda is lending the customer money
choices.why: The instalments are interest-free; the cost appears only if Varanda pays to receive early.

prompt: Varanda has a record December in profit and is short of cash in January. By the lesson, what is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: The profit figure is wrong
choices.why: Both can be right at once; profit and cash are recorded at different moments.

choices.text: Customers did not pay for what they bought
choices.why: They are paying, in instalments; nothing suggests default.

choices.text: Sales on instalments bring cash in slowly while suppliers want paying now
choices.why: Right: profit is booked in December, the cash arrives over months, and the Christmas stock was bought in October.

choices.text: The board took the profit out as dividends
choices.why: Possible in principle, but the lesson's point is the timing of instalments.

prompt: 3,568,000 visits and 44,600 orders. What is the online conversion rate, in percent to two decimals?
Online conversion falls from 1.25% to 1.05%, and the share of visits reaching a cart has not changed. Where does the lesson point?

choices.text: The products and prices on the page
choices.why: Those would show as fewer carts, and carts are unchanged.

choices.text: Marketing, which is bringing the wrong visitors
choices.why: Wrong visitors would put less in the cart; that step is unchanged.

choices.text: Delivery costs, payment or the checkout
choices.why: Right: if carts hold steady and orders fall, people are stopping between cart and payment.

choices.text: The average ticket
choices.why: The ticket is the size of an order; conversion is whether there is one.

prompt: Varanda's acquisition cost came out at about R$ 76 per new customer. What does the lesson warn about this number?

choices.text: It is too low to be believed for an online shop
choices.why: The lesson makes no claim about what is typical; the issue is how it was computed.

choices.text: It should be divided by all customers, not by new ones
choices.why: That would be a different measure; the warning is about the numerator.

choices.text: It includes the stores' marketing as well as the online shop's
choices.why: It uses only the R$ 2.15 million of online marketing.

choices.text: All online marketing is charged to new customers
choices.why: Right: some of it reached returning customers, so it is a rough number, useful year against year if computed the same way.

prompt: Online sales equal visits times conversion times the average ___, so a report showing only sales hides which of the three moved.
With cost of goods sold of R$ 55,370 thousand and average stock of R$ 9,480 thousand at cost, how many days of stock did Varanda hold, to one decimal?
hint: Stock divided by cost of goods, times 365.

prompt: Stock turned 5.8 times in 2025 and there were 62.5 days of stock. How are the two related?

choices.text: The same fact, one the inverse of the other
choices.why: Right: 365 divided by 5.8 turns is about 62.5 days.

choices.text: Turns measure the stores, days measure the warehouse
choices.why: Both are for the whole company's stock here.

choices.text: More turns means more days of stock
choices.why: The other way round: faster turns mean fewer days.

choices.text: They are unrelated, since one uses sales and the other uses stock
choices.why: Both use the cost of goods sold and the average stock.

prompt: Caio proposes holding more garden stock before summer so no store runs out. Which cost of that choice does the lesson say the sales data will never show?
hint: Turn the question round: what does the opposite choice cost?

choices.text: The money tied up in the extra stock
choices.why: That cost is visible: about R$ 152,000 for every extra day of stock.

choices.text: The warehouse space it takes
choices.why: Space is a recorded cost of operations.

choices.text: Nothing in his plan; it is the stock-outs of holding less that leave no trace
choices.why: Right: a sale that did not happen is in no record, which is why holding less looks cheaper than it is.

choices.text: The delivery costs to the stores
choices.why: Deliveries are recorded; the trucks' cost is in the warehouse line.

prompt: The tension in operations is service level against stock ___: more stock means fewer empty shelves and more money tied up.
hint: What holding stock does to the bank balance.

prompt: 103 people left Varanda in 2025, against an average headcount of 410. What was the annual turnover, in percent to one decimal?
A trade magazine reports 18% turnover for home retailers. Why does the lesson warn against comparing it with Varanda's 25.1%?

choices.text: Magazines are not a reliable source
choices.why: The lesson's warning is about definitions, not about who publishes.

choices.text: Nobody said which formula gave the 18%
choices.why: Right: leavers only, the average of hirings and leavings, exclusions — each gives a different rate.

choices.text: Turnover cannot be compared between companies of different sizes
choices.why: A rate is exactly what makes sizes comparable, if the definition is the same.

choices.text: Varanda's figure is monthly and the magazine's is annual
choices.why: Varanda's 25.1% is annual; its monthly average is 2.1%.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a turnover table for a store with eight employees, by month, needs care?

choices.text: Eight is too few for the rate to be accurate
choices.why: Small numbers are noisy, but the lesson's concern here is privacy.

choices.text: Store managers are not allowed to see HR data
choices.why: The lesson sets no such rule; it is about what a breakdown reveals.

choices.text: It identifies who left and when
choices.why: Right: aggregate before showing, and do not publish a breakdown small enough to point at somebody.

choices.text: Turnover should be reported only for the whole company, by law
choices.why: No law in the lesson says that; the rule is the analyst's judgement about identification.

prompt: Match each number to the function that watches it most closely.
Online sales fell 10% in a month. By this lesson, which of these could each explain it on its own? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sales are visits times conversion times ticket.

choices.text: Fewer visits
choices.why: Right: one of the three factors.

choices.text: A lower share of carts being paid
choices.why: Right: lower conversion through the last step.

choices.text: A smaller average order
choices.why: Right: the average ticket.

choices.text: More days of stock in the warehouse
choices.why: Stock held is not in the sales identity; it matters only if it causes a stock-out.

choices.text: A higher gross margin
choices.why: Margin is what is left from sales, not what makes them.

prompt: Otávio says: "Our 2.9% operating margin is fine, retail margins are always thin." Which question would this lesson have Lívia ask next?

choices.text: Whether the margin should be shown as a chart instead of a number
choices.why: The form is not the issue; what moves the margin is.

choices.text: What the margin of the online shop is compared with the stores'
choices.why: A fair question, but not the one the thin margin raises first.

choices.text: Which large flows could erase it, and how easily
choices.why: Right: a 5% rise in the cost of goods alone would take R$ 2.77 million of the R$ 2.86 million.

choices.text: Whether 2.9% is the gross or the net margin
choices.why: It is the operating margin; the gross margin is 43.5%.
